bugs.title: Messageboard spec is blocked on a file that no longer exists
bugs.body: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-05-messageboard-design.md carries `Status: design only. Blocked on the dispatcher (harness/dispatch.ts), which does not exist yet.` The dispatcher exists and is Gleam: harness/src/harness/dispatch.gleam. The dependency named in the status line was superseded, not satisfied, so a reader cannot tell whether the spec is still blocked. Posts are in fact half-built: dispatch.gleam logs them as events and routes nothing. Filed rather than fixed because docs/ needs asking.

bugs.title: Guard events do not say which worker was denied
bugs.body: guard.gleam:386 logs every decision as event/tool/decision and nothing else. Under `run --concurrency 3` all three guards write to one runs/<id>/events.jsonl, so a Deny cannot be attributed to a worker or a node. Rules already carries `holder`, the identity it locks under, so the guard knows; it just does not log it. Auto-filing bugs from guard denials depends on this, so it is a prerequisite rather than a nice-to-have.
bugs.resolution: guard.gleam now logs a node key alongside every decision (holder was already the node id; the doc comment just called it an identity), with event_fields extracted so it is testable without an HTTP server; commit 0451d47.

bugs.title: A parked attempt leaves its proof file on disk, untracked
bugs.body: Rule30/Proofs/EvolveLeftSecondDiagonal.lean was left on disk when Vesper's attempt was parked, untracked and not imported by Rule30/Proofs.lean. Filed as a question rather than a defect, because the evidence cuts both ways: Rowan reports the re-dispatch built that same file unchanged and the verifier passed it, so leaving it saved a proof rather than losing one. What is genuinely wrong is that the file's existence carries no signal — nothing distinguishes `abandoned debris` from `a correct proof whose attempt was mislabelled`. Resolve this one by deciding, not by deleting: wontfix with a reason is a good outcome here.

bugs.title: hit_ceiling treats allowed_warning as a closed window
bugs.body:
Reported by Rowan, agents/Rowan.md 2026-09-06T02:05:00Z, filed by Keel.

worker.gleam:871 `hit_ceiling` saw a rate_limit_event at 0.94 utilization against the 0.9 ceiling and treated the window as closed. The event's API status was `allowed_warning` — a warning, not a refusal. Combined with an errored turn this parked a finished attempt as `rate_limited`, and a rate-limited attempt stops the run from starting more, so one misread warning can halt a whole run.

Rowan's ruling on the fix: only an api_retry carrying `rate_limit`, or a status that is not `allowed*`, means the window is actually closed.
bugs.resolution: hit_ceiling now decodes rate_limit_info.status and only closes the window on a non-allowed* status or a rate_limit api_retry; commit 7c3fc4e. Follow-up commit f64d488 fixed decode.subfield making status required (a missing status was silently swallowed into Other instead of RateLimit); it now decodes with a "" default so a status-less event keeps the pre-status fail-closed behaviour.

bugs.title: posts is required by the report schema but optional in the decoder
bugs.body:
Reported by Rowan, agents/Rowan.md 2026-09-06T02:05:00Z, filed by Keel.

brief.gleam:80 lists `posts` in the report schema's `required` array; worker.gleam:60 decodes it with `decode.optional_field("posts", [], ...)`. The two disagree, and the CLI's side wins: it rejects the structured-output tool call before the Gleam decoder ever sees it. A report with no posts is the common case, so this fires often.

Cost, observed: Vesper proved evolve_left_second_diagonal in one shot 85 seconds in, omitted `posts`, and the turn became an error. The `proved` claim the parking code adjudicates first was inside the rejected tool call, so it never counted, and the attempt was parked as rate_limited (see hit-ceiling-misreads-allowed-warning). The proof was correct and had to be re-dispatched to be recorded.

Fix: drop `posts` from the schema's `required` list, or make schema and decoder agree either way.

Keel's note: this generalises. Any field in `required` that a worker may reasonably omit is this same bug. The bug board's own `bugs` field must NOT be added to `required` for exactly this reason — an empty array is the common case there too.
bugs.resolution: posts dropped from the report schema's required array, agreeing with the decoder's existing default of []; commit 7c3fc4e.

bugs.title: Offline test fixtures point repo_root at the live checkout
bugs.body:
Reported by Keel and Rowan; root cause framing is Rowan's.

The offline run fixtures inject a fake verifier and a fake index writer so a test never touches Rule30/Proofs.lean, but cfg.repo_root is still the real checkout. So a test worker's proof file is written into the same Rule30/Proofs/ directory live provers write to: `gleam test` has been observed leaving Rule30/Proofs/HarnessProbe.lean behind.

This is the same defect as the incident in agents/Rowan.md where a test fixture with a colliding file name deleted a live proof. Two symptoms, one cause. Rowan's framing, which is the right one: offline fixtures should not point repo_root at the live checkout at all. Fixing that removes both.

Until then the only protection is the rule that tests must not run during a live run, which is unenforceable across two checkouts.

bugs.title: Guard tests bind fixed ports and a bind failure kills the whole runner
bugs.body:
Three independent sightings in one night: Rowan's first `gleam test` in a worktree died with a supervisor kill at the same minute another suite ran in the main checkout; a transient Eaddrinuse appeared during the Task 0 run from a just-exited process; and again during the Task 1 fix round.

The guard tests bind fixed ports, and mist's bind failure takes the whole test runner down rather than failing one test. So a stray `erl` from a previous run, or a second checkout running its suite, turns into a total and confusingly-attributed failure.

Two candidate fixes were discussed. Keel and Rowan both prefer picking ports from a free range at test time over a one-suite-at-a-time rule: the rule is unenforceable across two checkouts, which is exactly how it was hit. A bind failure should also fail its own test rather than the runner.

bugs.title: hit_ceiling ignores a refusal that arrives below the utilization ceiling
bugs.body:
Found by the Task 0 reviewer while checking the fix for hit-ceiling-misreads-allowed-warning.

hit_ceiling gates on `utilization >=. ceiling && !starts_with(status, "allowed")`. A rate_limit_event carrying a genuinely refusing status at, say, 0.5 utilization therefore returns False and the window is treated as open. This preserves the behaviour that existed before that fix and the conjunction was deliberate, so it is not a regression — but it is the opposite misread living in the same predicate: the fixed bug over-parked on a warning, this one under-parks on a refusal.

Filed rather than fixed because the reviewer's advice was a board line, not a code change in that task, and because nobody has yet seen a refusing status below the ceiling in the wild. Decide it with evidence: check whether the API ever sends one.

bugs.title: Line-ending churn reports untouched files as modified
bugs.body:
Seven files Rowan committed with LF show as modified in a Windows checkout the moment anything touches them, with `git diff --numstat` reporting zero changed lines. They are stat-dirty, not different.

The cost is not the churn itself, it is that it disguises real changes. Mid-plan this looked like another session had written into the checkout, which is a serious thing to see, and it took a numstat to rule out. Agents are told to stage explicit paths and read `git diff --cached` precisely so unrelated work is not swept into a commit; that discipline is much harder when seven unrelated files are permanently listed as modified.

The fix is a `.gitattributes` pinning `eol=lf`, which Rowan identified in its notebook and correctly flagged as Dib's call rather than an agent's. Do not commit the churned files as a workaround: they have no content diff, so staging them would bake CRLF line endings into the repository instead.

bugs.title: A wall node that becomes an open leaf aborts the whole run
bugs.body:
Reported by Rowan, after seeding the DAG's first `wall` node (evolve_left_diagonals_isEventuallyPeriodic) on 2026-09-06.

`schedule.next_to_start` has no `Wall` case: it ranks a wall node like any other open leaf once its deps are proved. `dispatch.start` then calls `config.model_for(Wall, _)`, whose ladder is empty by design, and returns Error("ladder exhausted for `X` although it is an open leaf"). `fill` propagates that Error, so the whole run aborts — not just that node — and it will abort again on every subsequent run, because nothing marks the node unselectable. The message's own wording ("although it is an open leaf") shows the author expected this to be unreachable.

The spec is clear that wall means "do not attempt without decomposing", so the fix belongs in the scheduler, not in dispatch: a wall node is not an open leaf, because an open leaf is a task the scheduler can actually start. Right fix is a `Wall` case in `next_to_start` that filters it out, with a test that a wall leaf is skipped and the run continues to the next candidate.

Not yet reachable in practice: the wall node's deps are three unproved nodes deep. It becomes live the moment that tier closes.

bugs.title: Long node ids run into the status column in `gleam run -- status`
bugs.body:
Reported by Rowan on 2026-09-06.

The status table pads the id column to a fixed width, and the new diagonal nodes are longer than it. The line reads

  evolve_left_fourth_diagonal_isEventuallyPeriodicopen      S     P1

with the id and the status fused. Cosmetic, and only in the human-facing table — the DAG itself is fine — but `status` is the command a human reads to decide what to dispatch, so it is the one place the board should stay legible. Pad to the longest id present rather than to a constant.

bugs.title: A guard event says a command was denied but not which command
bugs.body:
Reported by Rowan, 2026-09-06, run 20260906T150452Z. Filed as a second sighting of guard-events-carry-no-node first, which was wrong twice over: that bug was already fixed in 0451d47, and my run was driven from a worktree pinned at 54d2f2b, so what I saw was the pre-fix code. The observation below is what survives once that is stripped out, and it is a different defect.

guard.event_fields logs node, event, tool and decision. 0451d47 added the node, which settles attribution. What is still absent is the command. A Deny therefore reads as `tool: Bash, decision: Deny(only 'lake build [modules]' and 'lake env lean <file>' are permitted...)` and never says what the worker actually tried to run.

Why that matters more than attribution did. The denial message names the rule, so a reader knows which rule fired, but not whether it should have: a worker reaching for `lake build --help` and a worker reaching for `rm -rf` produce byte-identical events. Deciding whether the guard is correctly tight or wrongly tight is exactly the judgement this project needs the log for, and that judgement needs the command.

It is also unrecoverable from anywhere else, which is the part that makes it worth fixing rather than working around. An *allowed* command survives in the turn-end stream events: the full `lake build Rule30.Proofs.EvolveRightEdge` appears five times in run 20260906T144745Z's record. A *denied* one is refused at PreToolUse, so no tool_use is ever emitted and nothing reaches the stream. The guard is the only component that sees the command at the moment it is refused, so the guard event is the only place it can be recorded.

Same dependent as the bug it came from: a bug auto-filed from a denial would carry no content to act on and no signature to dedupe two different denials apart.

Note for whoever fixes it: the command can carry secrets in general, though not under this grammar, which permits only lake invocations. Worth a moment's thought before logging it verbatim, not a reason to skip it.

bugs.title: A non-array bugs field still costs the whole report
bugs.body:
Found by the reviewer of Task 5 round 2, and deliberately left open rather than fixed in that round.

The promise the bug-reporting channel is built on: nothing a worker puts in `bugs` may ever cost the turn's proof outcome. Two rounds closed the per-element routes -- the array is now read as `decode.list(decode.dynamic)` and each element decoded independently with `list.filter_map`, so a malformed or wrong-typed entry is discarded and `outcome`, `notebook` and `journal` survive.

One route remains. If `bugs` is present but is not an array at all -- a string, an object -- then `decode.list(decode.dynamic)` itself fails, and that failure is not per-element, so it threads up and fails the whole `Report` decode. The proof outcome is lost exactly as in the original incident.

Probability is low: constrained decoding should produce an array or nothing. But `posts-required-in-schema-not-in-decoder` is the proof that 'should' is not 'does', and it cost a correct proof.

Fix: give the array decode a fallback so a non-array `bugs` degrades to an empty list rather than failing -- the same treatment the field already gets when absent. Small. Left for the quiet window because a live run was in flight and this needs the test suite.

bugs.title: A bug left claimed by a dead session has no way back
bugs.body:
Noticed while Rowan was fixing the same shape in agents/sessions.json, and it is inherited rather than invented: the board borrows dag.json's status vocabulary on purpose, `claimed` included, so that the one board idiom transfers.

It transferred the hazard too. The DAG has the same problem -- a dispatcher that crashes mid-attempt leaves a node `claimed` -- and the harness answers it with an explicit `reopen` command that refuses any status but `claimed`. The bug board has no equivalent. A Keel session that claims a bug and is then killed, times out, or exhausts its context leaves that bug claimed forever, and nothing will ever un-claim it.

Rowan's framing of the same class, which is the clearest statement of it: a contract whose correctness depends on graceful shutdown is a contract that will not hold, because agent sessions almost never shut down gracefully.

Not yet biting: nothing on the board is claimed, and there is one maintainer. It starts biting the moment claiming is used at all.

Two candidate fixes, and the second is probably right. Either add a `reopen` for bugs, mirroring the DAG's; or drop `claimed` from the board's statuses entirely, since with a single maintainer it conveys nothing that `open` plus a look at git does not. The second removes the hazard instead of managing it, at the cost of the idiom being slightly less parallel to the DAG.

bugs.title: A build lock timeout reaches the worker as a Deny, indistinguishable in kind from a forbidden command
bugs.body:
Observed live by Rowan in run 20260906T150452Z at concurrency 2.

Cadence, proving evolve_left_fifth_diagonal, ran `lake build` at 15:26:46Z while Vesper held the build lock, and got:

  {"tool":"Bash","decision":"Deny(build lock timeout)"}

The safety property is right and should not change: an AcquireBuild that times out must become a Deny, so a worker never proceeds believing it holds a lock it does not. The friction is what the worker is told.

A worker's brief says the only two commands it may run are `lake build` and `lake env lean`. So the one command it is explicitly permitted comes back denied, and the text is diagnostic rather than actionable — it names the internal condition, not the response. Nothing in it says the denial is transient, that another worker caused it, or that retrying is the correct move. A worker could reasonably read it as 'building is refused' and either abandon the node or thrash against a rule it cannot satisfy. It is the same message shape as the grammar denial, which is genuinely permanent and must not be retried.

Cadence recovered on its own — it retried and got AcquireBuild at 15:30:37Z — so this cost about four minutes rather than the node. That is the good case, not the guaranteed one, and the cost scales with concurrency: one build lock shared by three workers makes this the normal path rather than the unlucky one.

Suggested fix is the wording, not the mechanism: say that another worker holds the build lock and that the right move is to wait and run the same command again. A denial a worker can act on correctly is worth more than one that accurately names an internal state.

---

Keel's amendment, and it supersedes the fix suggested above.

**The fix is structural, not wording.** `Decision` currently has one `Deny(reason: String)` carrying every refusal, so "you may never do this" and "not right now" are the same value with different prose. That is why the two are indistinguishable to a worker — they are literally the same case, and no wording can separate them for long. The next person to add a third kind of refusal puts it in the same variant and the bug returns wearing new text.

Split the variant instead: a `Busy` (or `DenyTransient`) alongside `Deny`, with the message generated per case rather than passed in. The hook protocol only offers allow/deny at the wire, so a worker still sees a denial either way, but the Gleam type then makes it impossible to emit a transient refusal that reads like a permanent one. `event_fields` can also log which kind it was, which is what guard-events-do-not-record-the-denied-command wants for a different reason.

The safety property is untouched: a timed-out AcquireBuild still denies, because a worker proceeding while it believes it holds a lock it does not is the failure worth keeping.

**The text should still change, and say what to do rather than what happened.** "Another worker holds the build lock; wait a few seconds and run the same command again" is actionable. "build lock timeout" is a diagnosis addressed to whoever wrote the harness, which is the wrong audience — the reader is a worker with exactly two permitted commands, one of which just failed.

**The scaling argument is the reason to fix this, not the incident.** The incident came out fine: Cadence recovered in four minutes. One lock shared by three workers makes contention the normal path rather than the unlucky one, and a worker that reads a transient refusal as permanent abandons a node it could have proved. Abandonment is expensive and quiet — it costs a full attempt off the ladder and looks like a hard node rather than a harness defect, so it would be miscounted as difficulty in the calibration data as well.

bugs.title: An attempt the harness broke is scored as a hard node
bugs.body:
Observed by Rowan while filing build-lock-timeout-reads-as-a-permission-refusal, filed by Keel as the general case rather than the instance.

When a harness defect causes a worker to abandon, nothing distinguishes that from the node being hard. The attempt is recorded with outcome `abandoned`, it consumes a rung of the model ladder, and it lands in the size-calibration data as evidence of difficulty. So a harness bug does not merely cost one proof: it silently corrupts the signal the overseer uses to price every future node, and it does so in the direction that makes the node look worse than it is. The next dispatch at that node starts on a more expensive model for no reason.

Rowan's point, and it is the part that would take a long time to see from outside: this is invisible precisely because the record looks correct. An abandoned attempt is a normal thing. Nothing in the DAG says why.

The signal now exists and is unused. Since provers can file bugs in their end-of-turn report, an attempt that both abandoned AND filed a `blocks`-severity bug is very likely a harness failure rather than a hard node. Nothing correlates the two.

Candidate fixes, cheapest first. Record on the `Attempt` whether the worker filed a blocking bug, and exclude those attempts from calibration and from the ladder count -- an attempt the harness broke should not spend a rung. Or add an outcome distinct from `abandoned` for it. The first is smaller and uses data already being collected as of the bug-reporting channel.

Worth doing before the calibration numbers are trusted for anything, because the corruption is retroactive: the attempts already on the board cannot be re-scored.

--- AMENDED after Rowan refuted the proposed heuristic ---

The 'abandoned AND filed a blocks bug' correlation above is kept only as a weak secondary signal, because it misses the exact case that motivated this entry.

Rowan's objection, which is correct: a worker that receives Deny("build lock timeout"), reads it as a permanent rule, and gives up DOES NOT FILE A BUG. It has no complaint. It believes it hit a legitimate boundary and behaved correctly. The workers who file blocking bugs are the ones who noticed something was wrong, and a worker defeated by a harness defect it mistook for a rule is by definition one that did not notice. So the correlation is blind precisely where it is needed.

The inverse fails too, less badly: a worker can file a genuine blocks bug and still be beaten by a genuinely hard node, and excluding that attempt discards a real difficulty signal.

Better primary signal, and it needs the Decision split from build-lock-timeout-reads-as-a-permission-refusal: once the guard distinguishes transient from permanent refusals and event_fields logs which kind, the harness can observe 'this attempt received transient denials and then abandoned' without asking the worker anything. That is derived from outside the process by the component that actually knows. The guard is a reliable witness; a worker is not, especially about a failure it did not perceive as one.

This is the same principle Rowan and Keel arrived at independently earlier the same day, in agents/sessions.json and in the board's `claimed` status: where state must survive a session that dies without warning, derive it from outside the process rather than asking the process to report it.

Plan: guard-derived signal primary, filed-bug correlation secondary. Two weak signals failing in different directions beat one that fails in the direction that matters. This makes the Decision variant split load-bearing for three separate entries, which is an argument for doing it first.

Ownership, settled with Rowan: calibration is not separable from this. calibration_hits/calibration_total live in roster.gleam and the ladder count is failed_attempts in dispatch.gleam, both in harness/. Splitting it would put two agents in one area on one coherent change. Keel takes Attempt, failed_attempts and the roster calibration together; Rowan reviews whether the resulting numbers mean what the overseer needs them to mean.

RETROACTIVE, and not fixable: every attempt already recorded was scored under this defect, so the calibration figures quoted in agents/Rowan.md -- Vesper 2/3, and the five attempts of 2026-09-06 -- are contaminated to an unknown degree. Nobody is going to re-score them. Written down here so the first person to trust those numbers knows they predate the fix.

bugs.title: Nothing tells a session whether uncommitted work is live or orphaned
bugs.body:
Near-miss on 2026-09-06, no loss. Reported jointly: Keel found it, Rowan supplied the analysis that makes it a real bug rather than an anecdote.

WHAT HAPPENED. Keel found 192 uncommitted lines across all 14 files in Rule30/Proofs/ -- teaching docstrings, real work, existing in exactly one place. ListAgents showed two sessions that had been live forty minutes earlier were gone. Keel concluded the work might be orphaned by a dead session and stopped rather than tidying. It was in fact Rowan's, mid-verification.

THE DEFECT IS NOT THE WRONG CONCLUSION, IT IS THAT THE EVIDENCE CANNOT SUPPORT A RIGHT ONE. Rowan's framing: the two vanished sessions really were its provers, they really had ended, and a reader with only that evidence could not distinguish in-progress work from abandoned work. The shared checkout cannot tell 'being written' from 'left behind', and neither can any observer. `git status` shows that uncommitted work exists; nothing shows whose it is or how old it is.

WHY THE WINDOW EXISTS, AND WHY 'JUST COMMIT PROMPTLY' IS NOT THE FIX. Rowan's work sat uncommitted for about twenty minutes because it was running `lake build` between editing and committing. That is not carelessness, it is the verification step this project requires -- no agent, including the dispatcher, gets to declare a proof done by assertion. Any fix premised on committing sooner is asking people to commit unverified work, which is the one thing the project explicitly refuses. That tension is the actual content of this bug.

AUTO-COMMIT IS PROBABLY THE WRONG FIX, and both of us independently landed there. Half-finished work committed automatically now auto-pushes to a branch on a public remote under whatever identity is configured, which is worse than losing it.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY HELP is visibility rather than automation: something a session can consult to see uncommitted work it did not write, and how long it has been sitting. The first half exists in `git status`; the second half -- attribution and age -- does not exist anywhere. A session starting work in this checkout currently has no way to know it is about to step on someone.

THE MITIGATION THAT ACTUALLY WORKED, and it is worth keeping regardless of any fix: every implementer dispatched into this checkout is instructed to stage explicit paths only, and never to run `git add -A`, `git add .`, `git checkout` or `git restore` on any path. That discipline is what protected these 14 files while three agents worked around them.

RELATED: this is the other half of the problem Rowan fixed in agents/sessions.json. That fix removed the stale-row hazard -- state a dead session leaves behind that misleads a reader. This is the same class one layer down, and larger: state a dead session leaves behind that a reader cannot even classify.
